nature-clim-227.title: Putting a price on a warming world
nature-clim-227.text: How much will climate change cost, and who will pay? Economic analysis of climate change uses the tools and models of economics to estimate how large climate damages are and who bears them. It studies three bills at once: the cost of climate impacts, the costs and benefits of preventing climate change, and the cost of adapting to it. From those sums it can suggest which policies make the most economic sense. Mitigation means cutting the emissions that cause warming, and adaptation means adjusting to the warming that comes anyway. The toolkit has three main parts. Process-based models, described in {{ref:nature-clim-248}}, trace the links between the economy and the climate. Structural models, such as computable general equilibrium (CGE) models and cost-benefit models, represent how the whole economy fits together. Statistical, or econometric, methods estimate from data how weather and climate affect economic variables, either globally or in one sector. The economics of mitigation is one of the most contentious parts of climate policy. One reason is that ordinary economic signals miss much of the picture. The stock market, for example, underestimates or cannot value the social benefits of cutting emissions. The approach extends {{ref:nature-val-001}} to the harms described in {{ref:nature-eco-017}}.

nature-clim-222.title: Climate risk: when the old extremes no longer hold
nature-clim-222.text: In 2020 the World Economic Forum ranked climate change as the biggest risk to the economy and society. Climate risk is the chance that the impacts of climate change will harm societies or ecosystems. It comes in two broad kinds. Physical risks are direct blows, such as extreme weather. Transition risks are the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society. Risk can also come from the measures people take in response, not only from the changes themselves. Climate risk is harder to assess than ordinary hazard risk. The climate no longer stays within a stable range of extremes, so the past is a weaker guide. Scientists therefore lean on pictures of possible futures, described in {{ref:nature-clim-252}}, when they analyze it. They also group risks by sector: agriculture, water, cities, ecosystems, health and livelihoods. Two kinds of response can lower these risks. Adaptation adjusts to the changes and mitigation slows them, and the two can work together. Like every question of {{ref:nature-econ-772}}, climate risk deals in chances rather than certainties.

nature-clim-241.title: The social cost of carbon: pricing one more ton
nature-clim-241.text: What is the damage from one more ton of carbon dioxide worth? The social cost of carbon (SCC) answers in money, usually dollars. Putting climate effects into money terms lets policymakers weigh actions that raise or cut greenhouse gas emissions. The idea has old roots. Arthur Pigou proposed in 1912 to tax activities that cause negative externalities, harms that fall on people outside a deal, such as pollution. Today the SCC is widely used in regulatory impact analyses, cost-benefit assessments and climate policy. It is not itself a carbon price. Taxes and cap-and-trade schemes are separate tools, though the SCC can inform them. Its weakness is sensitivity. A few assumptions drive the answer, above all the discount rate, the damage function and climate sensitivity. The discount rate, explained in {{ref:nature-econ-745}}, sets how much future harm counts today. In the United States, values have swung from $6 per ton under Trump, using a 7% rate, to over $51 under Biden, using 3%. Economists, scientists and ethicists criticize the SCC for that volatility, for its ethics and for its dependence on assumptions. Some scholars argue that its one-extra-ton logic fits the climate crisis poorly, and that limits on total emissions may serve better.

nature-clim-270.title: Carbon accounting: keeping the books on emissions
nature-clim-270.text: No one can cut what they cannot count. Carbon accounting is a set of methods for measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organization emits. Organizations use it to set a baseline, choose reduction targets and track progress. It works at every scale, from companies and cities up to national greenhouse gas inventories. Standards such as the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and ISO 14064 sort emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 covers direct emissions, Scope 2 purchased energy, and Scope 3 the wider value chain. Scope 3 is often the largest share of a company's emissions and the hardest to report accurately. Accurate counts matter beyond the firm. Carbon credit markets depend on them, and investors use them to judge a company's climate risks. There is some evidence that programs requiring this accounting help lower emissions.

nature-clim-268.title: The Stern Review: the greatest market failure
nature-clim-268.text: On 30 October 2006, the economist Nicholas Stern released a 700-page review of the economics of climate change for the UK government. It called climate change the greatest and widest-ranging market failure ever seen. Its main conclusion was that the benefits of strong, early action far outweigh the costs of not acting. Without action, it estimated losses of at least 5% of global GDP each year, possibly 20% or more counting wider risks. It proposed investing 1% of global GDP a year. In 2008 Stern raised that to 2%, saying the Review had underestimated the risks and that warming was faster than expected. The most debated point was its near-zero pure rate of time preference, which counts future welfare almost as much as today's. Stern held it to be the only ethical choice. Some economists called the Review deeply flawed, while others, including Kenneth Arrow, judged its main conclusion justified. The disputes over its discount rate, damages and costs continue.

nature-clim-252.title: Climate scenarios: plausible stories about the future
nature-clim-252.text: Nobody can forecast the far future, but analysts can sketch the possibilities. A climate change scenario is a plausible picture of how the future might unfold, built on assumptions about the main forces driving climate change. Three key inputs are population, economic activity and new technology. Scenarios help test how well mitigation and adaptation will work over the long term. A baseline scenario is the reference case, against which an alternative such as a mitigation scenario is compared. Pathways are related but more concrete: a roadmap of the actions needed to make a scenario come true. One finding cuts against intuition. Economic growth has proved compatible with both rising and falling emissions, depending on efficiency, energy sources and the shift toward services. Countries use scenarios when drawing up adaptation plans and their nationally determined contributions, the climate pledges each country makes.

nature-clim-248.title: Integrated assessment models: the economy and the sky in one framework
nature-clim-248.text: Climate policy needs a tool that links factories to the atmosphere. Integrated assessment modelling tries to provide one, joining the main features of society and the economy with the biosphere and atmosphere in a single framework. Its goal is to inform policy-making, usually on climate change. Every climate integrated assessment model (IAM) includes economic processes and the processes that produce greenhouse gases. These models do not predict the future. Instead they estimate what possible scenarios look like. They come in two broad families. Process-based models map detailed pathways. Aggregate models add up the total costs of climate change and of mitigation. Cost-benefit IAMs such as DICE, PAGE and FUND are the main tools for calculating the social cost of carbon. The models have been severely criticized. Critics say they create an illusory sense of precision and handle justice poorly. They have also been accused of undervaluing wind and solar power while overvaluing bioenergy and carbon capture. Because the models exist to inform policy, such biases matter. Their treatment of uncertainty remains disputed as well.

nature-clim-267.title: Five possible worlds: the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
nature-clim-267.text: Will the world of 2100 be cooperative or divided, green or fossil-fueled? The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) offer five answers. They are scenarios of how global society and the economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. Each pairs a storyline of socio-economic development with data on population, urbanization and GDP per person. The five are SSP1 Sustainability, SSP2 Middle of the road, SSP3 Regional rivalry, SSP4 Inequality and SSP5 Fossil-fueled development. On their own they describe societies, not emissions. Run through integrated assessment models, they yield emissions scenarios under different climate policies. IPCC scenario names combine the pathway with the forcing, the extra warming push on the planet, in 2100. SSP2-4.5 is one example. The spread of outcomes is wide. Projected warming for 2081–2100 runs from 1.4 °C under SSP1-1.9 to 4.4 °C under SSP5-8.5. A 2025 assessment put median warming under current policies at about 2.7 °C by 2100. That is closest to SSP2-4.5, the middle of the road.

nature-clim-245.title: Marginal abatement cost: the price of the next cut
nature-clim-245.text: Cutting the first ton of pollution can be cheap, and cutting the last far more expensive. The marginal abatement cost is the cost of reducing pollution by one more unit. It applies the idea of marginal cost, the cost of one additional unit, to the next unit of pollution removed. Sometimes it is negative, when the low-carbon option is cheaper than business as usual. But it often rises steeply as more pollution is cut. A marginal abatement cost curve ranks the possible reductions by their cost. Policymakers use these curves to see how much abatement is possible at what cost, and carbon traders use them to model carbon prices. Studies worldwide find that more efficient buildings and renewables replacing fossil power are usually the cheapest cuts. The curves are contested. Critics fault their poor transparency and weak handling of uncertainty, timing, links between sectors and side benefits.

nature-clim-261.title: Cumulative emissions: the long memory of carbon
nature-clim-261.text: Carbon dioxide stays in the air for at least 150 and up to 1000 years, while methane disappears within about a decade. So responsibility for warming builds up over time. Cumulative emissions add up emissions over long periods to show who caused the build-up. Between 1890 and 2007 the United States caused 28% of energy-related CO2 emissions, the EU 23% and China 9%. Developed countries together caused 67.8%. Today's largest emitters are not always those with the highest historical emissions.

nature-clim-260.title: Where emissions come from, sector by sector
nature-clim-260.text: About two-thirds of the world's greenhouse gas emissions come from burning fuels for energy. Dividing emissions among the economic sectors that cause them shows the rest of the picture. Counted where they are produced, electricity generators make about 25% of global emissions. Among non-energy sources, agriculture adds 12% of the total, land use change and forestry 7%, industrial processes 6% and waste 3%. Power is strikingly concentrated: just 5% of the world's power plants produce almost three-quarters of the sector's carbon emissions.

nature-clim-262.title: Emissions inequality: the rich pollute more
nature-clim-262.text: Between 1990 and 2015, the richest 1% of people caused twice as much carbon emissions as the poorest 50%. That gap is emissions inequality, driven by a strong link between income and emissions per person. The wealthiest 5% were responsible for 37% of the absolute rise in global emissions. Between countries the pattern repeats. Yearly emissions per person in industrialized countries are typically up to ten times those in developing countries.

nature-clim-232.title: What adapting to climate change will cost
nature-clim-232.text: Every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion. Returns like that explain why economists study the costs of adaptation: the costs of planning, preparing for, enabling and carrying out adjustment to climate change. The benefits are measured as the damages adaptation avoids. More resilient infrastructure in developing countries would yield an average of $4 of benefit for each $1 invested. The bills are large. A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion a year up to 2030. Another 2023 study, based on national plans from 85 countries, put their annual needs at US$387 billion. Both estimates are highly uncertain.

nature-clim-230.title: The bill for cutting emissions
nature-clim-230.text: Economists estimate the cost of mitigation, cutting greenhouse gas emissions or enlarging the carbon sinks that absorb them, at between 1% and 2% of GDP. That is far less than the IMF's estimate of over $5 trillion a year in fossil fuel subsidies. A 2024 study found that keeping warming below 2 °C may cost about 1% of world GDP a year. Yet it could prevent losses of 10–20% of GDP by mid-century. Estimates depend on the baseline scenario, the way costs are modeled and assumptions about future policy. Models assuming perfect markets and policy give low costs. Relaxing those assumptions raises the estimates, while faster technological learning lowers them. Early, well-planned action keeps costs down, and delayed global cooperation raises them. Costs are higher in carbon-intensive, fossil-fuel-exporting and poorer regions when all regions face one carbon value. Marginal abatement costs vary by country, sector and time, so policymakers can compare measures.

nature-clim-233.title: Weighing climate costs and benefits in dollars
nature-clim-233.text: Can the welfare of people a century from now be weighed against today's bills? Cost-benefit analysis of climate change tries, turning an action's good and bad effects into money values. Most such analyses run on aggregate integrated assessment models built for the purpose. Costs and benefits are valued by willingness to pay or willingness to accept, then discounted to present values. A policy usually passes the Kaldor–Hicks test: the winners could compensate the losers and still come out ahead. Climate strains this logic. Future generations who gain from mitigation cannot compensate the present generation that pays for it. Valuing impacts on ecosystems and human health is also hard, which makes the method controversial. It may be unsuitable for judging mitigation as a whole. It is still useful for comparing a 1.5 °C target with 2 °C.

nature-clim-228.title: How much a warmer world costs the global economy
nature-clim-228.text: Losses from extreme weather, climate and water events rose sevenfold from the 1970s to the 2010s. One study put the share attributable to climate change at an average US$143 billion a year between 2000 and 2019. The global economic costs of climate change add up predicted impacts across all market sectors, plus non-market harm to ecosystems and health. Estimates rise non-linearly as the global average temperature rises. The 2022 IPCC report found that with about 4 °C of warming and little adaptation, annual global GDP might be 10–23% lower by 2100. With low warming and more adaptation, the reduction was 1–8%. Holding warming to 1.5 °C rather than 3.66 °C is estimated to cut total damages by 90%. Climate impacts also add to inflation through higher insurance premiums, energy costs and food prices. Yet global estimates handle tipping points poorly and leave out well-being and who bears the losses.

nature-clim-259.title: How much carbon stays in the air, and for how long
nature-clim-259.text: For six decades, the share of each year's carbon dioxide emissions that stays in the air has held steady at 0.45. That airborne fraction means 0.55 is taken up by carbon sinks within the first year. A gas's atmospheric lifetime is the time needed to restore equilibrium after a sudden change in its concentration. Both measures are set by the balance between a gas's sources and sinks. The balance can shift. In high-emission scenarios, sinks become less effective, so the airborne fraction rises.

nature-clim-223.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three roots of climate risk
nature-clim-223.text: Global disaster losses have grown mainly because more people and wealth are exposed, though human-caused climate change also plays a part. The IPCC captures this in a framework where climate risk arises from three interacting factors. A hazard is the climate event itself. Exposure is who and what lies in its path. Vulnerability measures how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed, formally their propensity to be adversely affected. Each factor may be uncertain in both size and likelihood. Because risk comes from their interaction, adaptation can lower it by acting on all three.

nature-clim-247.title: DICE: William Nordhaus's model of climate and the economy
nature-clim-247.text: In a 1992 Cowles Foundation discussion paper, William Nordhaus proposed the DICE model. It combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change. A regional variant, RICE, followed in 1996. Its central assumption is that externalities create costs missing from prices, which government must add. It discounts the future at the market return on capital, around 4% on average. The US Environmental Protection Agency uses it as one of three main models for the social cost of carbon. Its answers have shifted. In 2020, a rerun with updated science and discount rates put the optimal goal below 2.0 °C of warming, not the 3.5 °C Nordhaus first found. A 2020 paper with an updated damage function found around 2 °C optimal, depending on climate sensitivity. DICE treats innovation as external. A variant with induced technical change favors strong early investment in mitigation. Critics attack its sensitivity to assumptions and its discount rate.

nature-clim-265.title: The Kaya identity: four levers behind every ton of CO2
nature-clim-265.text: Total carbon dioxide emissions can be written as four numbers multiplied together. The Kaya identity, developed by the Japanese energy economist Yoichi Kaya, uses population, GDP per person, energy used per unit of GDP, and emissions per unit of energy. In theory the factors cancel out. The point is practical: the identity lets emissions be estimated from readily available data. It is a form of the I = PAT equation for environmental impact, from Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren. It also shows the levers for cutting emissions, notably energy per unit of GDP and emissions per unit of energy. It plays a core role in building future emissions scenarios in the IPCC Special Report on Emissions Scenarios. Energy used per unit of GDP has generally declined worldwide, through efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.

nature-clim-251.title: Carbon lock-in: why fossil systems are hard to leave
nature-clim-251.text: Low-carbon technologies that are already cost-effective often spread slowly, a puzzle called the climate policy paradox. Carbon lock-in helps explain it. Gregory Unruh coined the term in a 1999 doctoral thesis for the self-reinforcing inertia of large fossil-fuel energy systems. Technology networks grow together with the institutions and habits that benefit from them, fed by increasing returns to scale. The result is a form of the pattern described in {{ref:nature-pol-038}}. Car-based transport and fossil-fuel power systems are examples. A 2007 report sorted the barriers into three kinds: cost-effectiveness, financial and legal, and intellectual property. The risk is current. Building new natural gas infrastructure threatens fresh lock-in and stranded assets, investments that lose their value early.

nature-clim-239.title: The side effects of cutting emissions
nature-clim-239.text: Cutting emissions can also save lives. Fewer deaths and less illness are potentially a major side benefit of mitigation. Economists call such effects, beyond any effect on the climate, ancillary benefits. Some side effects help and some hurt, so they can either lower or raise the estimated costs of mitigation.

openers.clim: Emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide does damage that economists try to price in dollars. This part of the course follows that effort, from estimates of how large climate damages are and who bears them to the chance that climate change will harm societies and ecosystems. It meets the tools involved: plausible pictures of the future, models that join the economy to the atmosphere, and methods for counting what an organization emits. It also asks who is responsible, because emissions added up over long periods, and the gap between rich and poor emitters, tell an uneven story.
openers.the-economics-of-climate-change: In October 2006 the economist Nicholas Stern released a 700-page review of the economics of climate change for the UK government. This chapter takes up the questions it made famous. How much damage does one more ton of carbon dioxide cause, and what does it cost to cut pollution by one more unit? Economists answer with scenarios of how society and the economy might change up to 2100, and with models that link the economy to the biosphere and atmosphere. Their answers keep returning to responsibility, since rich people and long-industrialized countries have emitted far more than the poor.
